lesson.title: Coaxial Cable: Wrapping the Signal in Its Own Shield
lesson.summary: Coaxial cable protects its signal with a built in metallic shield rather than relying on twisting alone, trading flexibility and cost for far better noise immunity and higher achievable bandwidth over a single physical medium.
lesson.body:
Twisted pair cable, from the previous chapter, defends against interference using geometry: twisting two wires so that noise hits both roughly equally and cancels out differentially. Coaxial cable takes a more direct approach, wrapping the signal carrying conductor in an actual physical shield. A coaxial cable is built from the inside out: a single copper conductor runs down the center, surrounded by an insulating layer called the dielectric, which is in turn surrounded by a metallic shield, typically a woven braid, a foil layer, or both, and the entire assembly is wrapped in an outer protective jacket. The name comes from the fact that the central conductor and the outer shield share the same central axis.

That outer shield does two jobs at once. It keeps external electromagnetic interference from reaching the inner conductor in the first place, rather than merely canceling interference after both wires have already picked it up the way twisted pair does, and it also keeps the cable's own signal from radiating outward and interfering with anything nearby. Because the shielding is so much more direct and complete than twisted pair's geometric cancellation trick, coaxial cable achieves noticeably higher usable bandwidth and can run signals over longer distances before the signal degrades past usability, at the cost of being noticeably thicker, heavier, and less flexible to install than twisted pair, and generally more expensive per unit length as well.

Coaxial cable has a characteristic impedance, the effective resistance the cable presents to a changing signal, determined by the physical dimensions and materials of the conductor, dielectric, and shield, and it is important to match that impedance correctly between a cable and the equipment connected to it, since a mismatch causes part of the signal to reflect back toward the source rather than continuing on to the receiver. Two impedance values show up repeatedly in practice: 50 ohm coaxial cable, historically used in early Ethernet installations, and 75 ohm coaxial cable, the standard for cable television and video distribution.

You have likely encountered coaxial cable already without necessarily thinking about the physical layer underneath it: it is the cable running into a cable television set top box, and it is also part of the backbone of cable internet service, where a hybrid fiber coaxial (HFC) network runs fiber optic cable, the medium in the next chapter, from the provider's facility to a neighborhood junction and then finishes the last stretch to individual homes over coaxial cable. Older Ethernet standards also ran directly over coax: 10BASE5, nicknamed Thicknet for its thick, rigid cable, and 10BASE2, nicknamed Thinnet for a thinner and more flexible variant, both carried 10 megabit Ethernet over coaxial cable before twisted pair wiring took over as the dominant choice for local area networks.
